title: Matthew 21:12–17
context: After entering Jerusalem as Zechariah’s King, Jesus goes straight to the temple. He drives out commerce, heals the blind and lame, and receives the children’s Hosanna—while priests and scribes grow indignant—so Passion Week begins with cleansing, mercy, and contested praise.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 21:12–17.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He cast out all that sold and bought - Doves and oxen for sacrifice. He had cast them out three years before, John ii, 14; bidding them not make that house a house of merchandise. Upon the repetition of the offense, he used sharper words. In the temple - That is, in the outer court of it, where the Gentiles used to worship.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 21:12–17)

reformed.quote: Matthew says that the city was moved, in order to inform us that the transaction did not take place secretly, or by stealth, but in the presence of all the people, and that the priests and scribes were not ignorant of it. Under this despicable aspect of the flesh the majesty of the Spirit was apparent; for how would they have endured that Christ should be conducted into the city, attended by the splendor of royalty, with so great danger to themselves, if they had not been seized with astonishment?
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 21:12–17)

verses.text: Jesus entered into the temple of God and drove out all of those who sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus enters the temple and acts with holy zeal: sellers and buyers are driven out; tables and seats overturned. The house meant for God is being cleared of traffic that crowds out prayer.

Arminians hear a moral summons. Grace exposes what distorts worship and calls people to turn. The King’s anger is not capricious; it presses a responsible response—leave exploitation and make room for God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The temple scene is deliberate royal judgment. Jesus’ driving out and overturning display His authority over Israel’s worship center at the start of Passion Week.

Reformed readers see providence and lordship together: the Son cleanses what belongs to His Father. Commerce that hindered true worship meets the King’s appointed confrontation—history moving on schedule toward the cross.

verses.text: He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus grounds His act in Scripture: “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” yet they have made it “a den of robbers.” Isaiah’s hope and Jeremiah’s indictment meet in one sentence.

Arminian pastoral reading stresses sincere invitation beneath the rebuke. God still names His house a place of prayer; grace calls hearers to repent of robbery—spiritual and economic—and return to communion with Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
“It is written” frames the cleansing as fulfillment of God’s Word, not private opinion. The temple’s true purpose and Israel’s present distortion stand under biblical judgment.

Christ speaks as Lord of the house. Hardness that turns prayer into plunder is exposed by Scripture itself; the King’s word both condemns the den and vindicates God’s holy claim.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Scripture naming the temple a house of prayer against a den of robbers. Arminians emphasize an earnest call to repent and restore prayerful worship; Reformed commentators often stress Christ’s authoritative judgment fulfilling God’s Word against hardness that has corrupted the house.

verses.text: The lame and the blind came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Immediately the blind and lame come to Jesus in the temple, and He heals them. Cleansing makes space for mercy; the King who drives out robbers welcomes the needy.

Arminians linger on the approach: they came, and He healed. Assisting grace draws the weak toward Christ; healing answers a seeking. The temple becomes again a place where the broken find the Savior.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mercy follows judgment in the same sacred space. Those shut out by custom or weakness are healed by the Messiah in the temple itself.

The Lord’s sovereign kindness is not delayed by human schemes. He who overturns tables also opens eyes and strengthens limbs—signs that the true King restores what God intends His house to be.

verses.text: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children who were crying in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the son of David!” they were indignant,
verses.arminianNotes:
Priests and scribes see wonderful works and hear children cry, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”—yet they are indignant. Light and praise provoke resentment instead of faith.

Grace can be resisted. The same temple that hosts healing and Hosanna becomes a place of stubborn refusal. Responsible unbelief hardens when invitation is met with envy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Wonderful deeds and children’s Messianic praise should compel worship; leaders answer with indignation. Matthew exposes hearts closed under judgment.

God may grant clear signs and true confession from little ones while the religious elite stiffen. Hardness here is not surprise outside providence; it advances the conflict that will lead to the cross.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat indignation at healing and Hosanna as tragic unbelief. Arminians emphasize a grace resisted by responsible refusal; Reformed readers emphasize hardness under judgment—God’s clear witness advancing His purpose even through leaders’ opposition.

verses.text: and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Did you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies, you have perfected praise’?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Leaders challenge Jesus: “Do you hear what these are saying?” He answers Yes—and cites Psalm 8: God has prepared praise from infants and nursing babies. The children’s Hosanna is not noise to silence but worship God intended.

Classical Arminians rejoice that God delights in responsive praise, even from the small. Grace opens mouths; Scripture legitimates their confession. Adults who refuse are summoned to learn from the little ones.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus affirms the children’s cry and roots it in Psalm 8: God Himself has prepared this praise. The question “did you never read?” indicts learned unbelief.

Praise is God’s preparation before it is human performance. Infants become instruments of ordained worship; the King receives what the Father has appointed, whether priests approve or not.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm that the children’s Hosanna is God-approved praise from Psalm 8. Arminians typically stress grace enabling welcomed confession that summons adults to join; Reformed interpreters underline that God has prepared the praise—sovereign appointment using infants to shame resistant leaders.

verses.text: He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and camped there.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus leaves them and lodges in Bethany outside the city. Withdrawal is not defeat; it is purposeful distance after confrontation.

Grace does not always remain where it is scorned. The open invitation of the day stands; those left behind must reckon with a King who will return—and with their response to cleansing, healing, and praise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus departs to Bethany for the night. The day’s work—cleansing, healing, contested praise—ends under His timing, not theirs.

The King is never trapped by indignation. Providence orders both presence and departure; Passion Week advances as He chooses, lodging where the Father’s plan places Him until the appointed hour.
